description:
About Us: We are a 100% newbie crew with massive ambition

What we're looking for: If you are a Coder or Designer looking for a fun, stress-free team that already has the business strategy, research, and 30-second video pitch completely covered, hop aboard our mission!
summary:
On Mars, rovers get stuck and wheels break. In 2009, NASA's Spirit rover was permanently trapped in soft soil at Troy, while sharp rocks damaged Curiosity's aluminum wheels. 

APOGEE is an interactive web game that turns these aerospace engineering trade-offs into an intuitive, hands-on simulation. Instead of passive quiz questions, players experience the complete mission loop: Design → Plan → Drive → Science → Report. 

Players build custom rovers within strict mass and budget limits, choosing between Lightweight, Wide Traction, or Reinforced wheels. In our playable showcase, "The Dune Crossing", players plot waypoints with real-time energy (EU) and risk forecasts, then manually drive the rover across Mars using WASD. Take the sandy shortcut with light wheels? The rover bogs down in a safety stop. Equip heavy wide traction wheels? You conquer the dunes and transmit 60 Science Score home.

Grounded in real NASA data—from the 24.6-hour Martian sol daylight cycle to RIMFAX subsurface radar—APOGEE runs natively in any browser with zero installs. Backed by 11 automated engine tests, APOGEE makes space mission design tangible through trial and error.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?
    APOGEE is a 3D web game where you plan, build, and drive a Mars rover. You pick a landing site, customize your rover within weight and budget limits, and drive on Mars in real time to scan for sand traps, collect samples, and swap parts at your base.
  2. What benefits does it have?
    It lets players feel real engineering trade-offs, like how heavy parts drain battery or get stuck in sand, or even just recharging battery and transmitting information can lead to the failure of the mission. It works right in a web browser with simple visual bars, giving students a risk-free way to test designs and learn from mistakes.
  3. What is the intended impact of the project?
    It teaches students that real space missions cannot just max out every stat because every upgrade costs weight, power, or money. Teachers can easily use its 15-minute missions in class to explain resource management and space engineering.
  4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
    We used TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Tailwind CSS. We also used Vite, Node.js, GitHub, and AI tools to speed up coding and 3D prototyping.
  5. How is your project creative?
    It connects pre-launch budget planning on Earth directly to survival on Mars, letting you scavenge crash scrap to craft and swap parts at your base. Swapping gear visually changes the 3D rover and its driving physics live, while scanning sends a 3D radar wave across the ground to reveal hidden traps.
  6. What factors did your team consider?
    We grounded the physics in real NASA missions, such as Spirit's sand traps, Perseverance's radar, and rocket weight limits. We also replaced complex math with simple color-coded gauges for beginners, and generated the 3D terrain via code so it runs smoothly on school laptops.
